title: The Three Voices Inside You
hook: The dosage question is simple until the nurse's answer changes voices halfway through.
counterintuition: The fastest read comes before personality judgment. Listen for the state speaking right now, because a grown adult can move from Adult fact to Parent rule before one sentence is finished.
tryThisNow: Replay one tense sentence from today. Mark only its state: Parent rule, Adult data, or Child reaction. Leave the solution alone for now.
keyTakeaway: Before you answer the words, hear the ego state behind them: Parent rules, Adult data, or Child feeling will each pull a different reply from you.

breakdown.fastRead:
"Can I ask why the order changed from 5 to 2.5?" The junior nurse is pointing at a laminated medication chart, and Sarah can feel her first answer forming. It begins with the dose history. Then it reaches for, "You should know this by now." She catches the turn before it leaves her mouth.

That catch is the first skill. Parent, Adult, and Child are not three people inside you; they are three registers a single sentence can wear. Adult handles the dose. Parent adds the rule. Child carries the old sting of being challenged.

Hear the voice before you answer the words.
breakdown.deepRead:
Camille is standing in a Paris product room while a pale checkout screen fills the glass wall. The junior designer has missed the same abandoned-cart pattern twice. Camille has the data open. She also has a sentence ready that would land like a school report: you should have caught this.

The Parent state is made from absorbed authority. It can be Critical Parent, sharp and corrective, or Nurturing Parent, warm and still quietly telling another person what to feel. Adult is different. Adult looks at what is here now, takes in new information, and changes course when the facts change. Child is the grown body's old emotional life: curiosity, hurt, play, compliance, rebellion, and the clever little workarounds learned around authority.

Camille points to the drop-off graph instead.

That small physical move keeps the conversation in Adult. The issue is no longer Camille's disappointment or the designer's shame. It is the third screen in the prototype, the payment field, the fifty-one percent drop after shipping address. The work can begin because the state in the room did not change the subject.

The hard part is that state shifts are often unchosen. A person sliding from Adult into Parent in the middle of a sentence is not usually deciding to slide. The shift happens. The first gain is recognition, not control. You hear the register change, and that half-second gives you a cleaner next sentence.
breakdown.fullRead:
You are holding your phone above the counter while three gray dots pulse in the family chat. Thomas's sister has asked who is taking their father to the cardiology appointment. The practical answer is 2:30, west entrance, bring the orange prescription bottle. His thumbs are ready to type something older: nice of you to ask after making every decision alone.

Nothing about the appointment created that sentence. The sentence came from a younger place.

The Parent-Adult-Child ego-state model is useful because it stays visible. Parent sounds like rules, judgments, permissions, and shoulds. It may scold, or it may soothe in a way that still puts one person above another. Adult sounds plainer. It asks what is known, what is missing, what has changed, and what must be decided now. Child sounds like original feeling: delight, shame, defiance, fear, play, and the old strategies that once kept a smaller person safe.

Thomas sends the appointment time only. He does not become wiser in that moment. He simply refuses to let the wrong state answer.

A direct question: if you replay one difficult exchange from the last week, where did the voice change? Not where did the facts change. Where did the sentence put on a rule, a wound, or a plea?

That question also keeps the model from turning into a personality label. A person is not "a Parent" or "a Child." They are in a state for a moment. Anke can sit in a cold tenant association room and hear an older member say, "We have always paid roof invoices before plumbing." The tone is Parent, but the invoice date may still be useful Adult information. If Anke attacks the tone, the room becomes smaller. If she asks for the date, she keeps the usable fact and leaves the rule voice unfed.

Two distortions matter: contamination and exclusion. Contamination happens when one state dresses as another. A prejudice can arrive dressed as an Adult fact, and a fear can arrive dressed as caution. Exclusion happens when a state is cut off: no play from Child, no moral limit from Parent, no present-tense checking from Adult. Neither problem is solved by pretending Adult should run every minute of life. A person with no Child is not healthy; they are flattened.

Diego sees the kinder version on a muddy football sideline. After a second missed penalty kick, he almost says, "You should be proud of yourself." The line sounds gentle. It is still Parent, because it tells the child what feeling is permitted. Diego changes the question: "What did you notice about your plant foot?" Now the child can look at the ground, the ball, the body, the next kick.

The model does not give you a remote control. It gives you a microphone. You begin to hear which voice is in the room, including your own, before the old reply completes itself. That is smaller than mastery and more useful than blame.

A clean next sentence often begins with hearing who was about to speak.

examples.title: Sarah Revises the Dose Reply

planSpec.domain: hospital shift handoff after a medication near-miss
planSpec.audience: a charge nurse deciding how to respond to a junior nurse who asks a clean dosage question
planSpec.stakes: patient safety, shame, and whether the room stays factual
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sarah hears her own first reply start as data and end as scolding, stops before the last clause, and restates the dose check in Adult language.

examples.scenario: "Can I ask why the order changed from 5 to 2.5?" The question hangs over the nurses station at 6:17 a.m. Sarah is the charge nurse, standing under the fluorescent task light with a laminated medication chart and a half-filled incident form. Her answer starts with the patient's kidney numbers, then swerves toward, "you should know this." She must decide whether to finish the scold or return to the dose.
examples.whatToDo: Stop before the rule voice lands. Say the lab value, the revised order, and the check-back step. Keep the exchange in Adult language so the nurse can verify the dose without shame.
examples.whyItMatters: The patient needs current data more than the room needs a hierarchy lesson. Once Sarah shifts into Parent, the junior nurse starts managing shame instead of checking medication.

examples.title: Camille Points to the Cart Drop

planSpec.domain: Paris product design critique for a flawed checkout screen
planSpec.audience: a design lead whose feedback can either teach the interface problem or shame the designer
planSpec.stakes: whether the junior designer learns the pattern or only learns to hide draft work
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille points to the abandoned-cart data instead of saying the designer should have known better.

examples.scenario: The projector throws a pale checkout form across the glass wall in Camille's Paris studio. A junior designer stands beside a sticky-note cluster while the abandoned-cart graph sits open on the laptop. Camille can already hear the sentence that would turn the critique into a lesson in obedience. Before the prototype review continues, she has to choose between pointing at the person and pointing at the payment-field drop.
examples.whatToDo: Point to the graph and ask what changed on the third screen. Keep the problem attached to the prototype click path, not to the designer's worth or maturity.
examples.whyItMatters: Adult feedback gives the designer something to test. Parent feedback makes the designer defend status, which hides the checkout pattern everyone needs to see.

examples.title: Thomas Sends the Appointment Time

planSpec.domain: family group text about an elderly parent's appointment
planSpec.audience: an adult son pulled between practical scheduling and old sibling rank
planSpec.stakes: a simple appointment can become a childhood argument in six messages
planSpec.requiredBeat: Thomas notices that his thumbs are answering his sister from the twelve-year-old who hated being corrected, then writes the appointment time only.

examples.scenario: You are holding the phone over the counter while three gray dots blink in the muted group chat. Thomas's sister asks who is taking Dad to cardiology, and the shared calendar invite is already open beside an orange prescription bottle. His thumbs reach for the old sibling reply. He must decide whether to answer from the twelve-year-old who hated correction or from the adult with the appointment time.
examples.whatToDo: Send the time, entrance, and medication reminder only. If the old rank fight wants a sentence, leave it unsent until the practical exchange is complete.
examples.whyItMatters: The family needs coordination. The Child state needs to settle an older score. Mixing them turns a calendar detail into a childhood argument with new punctuation.

examples.title: Anke Separates the Rule from the Date

planSpec.domain: tenant association budget meeting in a cold community room
planSpec.audience: a volunteer treasurer trying to stay in Adult while an older member speaks in Parent rules
planSpec.stakes: a repair fund vote may fail because the tone pulls everyone backward
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anke separates the member's rule-tone from the useful number hidden inside it and asks for the invoice date.

examples.scenario: The room smells of wet coats and copier toner before anyone sits down. Anke, the volunteer treasurer, has the roof repair invoice beside a coffee urn and six folding chairs. "We always pay roof work first," Mr. Voss says. "That is how responsible people do it." Anke hears the Parent rule and the useful clue inside it. Her next move has to choose a target: the tone or the invoice date.
examples.whatToDo: Ask for the invoice date and payment deadline. Let the rule voice pass without taking the bait, then put the useful number on the repair fund sheet.
examples.whyItMatters: A Parent tone can carry an Adult fact. If Anke argues with the posture, the room debates respect. If she extracts the date, the vote gets information.

examples.title: Diego Changes the Sideline Question

planSpec.domain: youth football sideline after a missed penalty kick
planSpec.audience: a coach whose comfort can still come from Parent if it tells the player what to feel
planSpec.stakes: whether a child gets present information or a borrowed script about toughness
planSpec.requiredBeat: Diego sees that his gentle line still commands the child to feel proud, then asks what the player noticed about his plant foot.

examples.scenario: It took Diego until the second missed kick to hear the order inside his kindness. The muddy penalty spot is chewed up, the substitution card is folded in his palm, and a team water crate rattles behind him. He almost says, "You should be proud for trying." The player is staring at the ground. Diego hears Nurturing Parent in the line and changes course.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what the player noticed about his plant foot. Offer care without telling him what feeling is allowed, then bring attention back to the next kickable detail.
examples.whyItMatters: A warm order is still an order. The player can use information about his foot; he cannot use a borrowed feeling that makes the coach comfortable.

examples.title: Aanya Names the Next Document

planSpec.audience: a legal-aid coordinator trying not to let an applicant's panic become her own Parent rescue script
planSpec.stakes: one wrong tone can turn an adult client into someone being managed
planSpec.requiredBeat: Aanya notices the urge to soothe and instead names the next document needed in present-tense terms.

examples.scenario: What changes when a kind voice starts telling someone how they should feel? Aanya is at a Toronto immigration clinic with a folder of translated documents, an intake checklist, and a numbered waiting ticket on the desk. The applicant is panicking over a missing date. Aanya feels the rescue script rise, soft and managerial, then notices it before it becomes the room's voice.
examples.whatToDo: Name the one document still needed and the next appointment window. Keep your tone steady, but do not tell the applicant what feeling to have.
examples.whyItMatters: Rescue can pull an adult client into Child position. Present-tense information keeps dignity in the room while still reducing the practical uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A clinic supervisor hears herself about to answer a nurse's dosage question with, "You should know this by now." Which ego state has started to take over the reply?
choices: Parent, because the sentence is turning current information into a rule and judgment.
Adult, because she knows the correct dose and wants accuracy.
Child, because she is speaking to someone younger in the hierarchy.
questions.explanation: The dose data may be Adult, but the should-and-judgment turn is Parent. Accuracy alone does not make the whole reply Adult, and hierarchy by age or rank is not what defines Child.

questions.prompt: During a budget call, a manager says, "The supplier raised prices 4 percent, so we need a new estimate by Friday." What makes this closest to Adult?
choices: It avoids emotional words, which means no ego state is active.
It works from current data, names a constraint, and can update if the estimate changes.
It gives an instruction, so it must be Parent rather than Adult.
questions.explanation: Adult handles present facts and revisable decisions. A calm tone alone is not enough, and an instruction can still be Adult when it follows from current information.

questions.prompt: A sibling asks for the appointment time. You feel a sharp old line arrive about always being treated like the unreliable one. What is the cleanest first move?
choices: Send the old line so the hidden resentment does not leak out later.
Explain the whole family pattern before sharing the appointment detail.
Send the time and location first, while recognizing that the old line belongs to Child.
questions.explanation: The practical exchange needs Adult information. Naming the old pull internally helps keep Child from running the reply; acting it out or analyzing the family first changes the task.

questions.prompt: A design lead thinks, "Only careless people miss a drop-off this obvious," while reviewing a checkout flow. Which response keeps the critique in the right state?
choices: Point to the abandoned-cart graph and ask what changes on the screen where users quit.
Say the careless line gently so it feels supportive rather than harsh.
Avoid the issue until the designer notices it alone.
questions.explanation: Pointing to the graph keeps attention on present evidence. A gentle insult is still Parent judgment, and silence leaves the observable product problem untouched.

questions.prompt: A volunteer treasurer hears an older member speak in a bossy rule tone but also mention that the roof invoice may be due tomorrow. What should she do with the mixed signal?
choices: Ignore the invoice detail because the tone proves the speaker is in Parent.
Challenge the bossy tone first so the group learns better meeting norms.
Separate the useful date from the rule tone and ask for the deadline.
questions.explanation: A Parent delivery can contain Adult information. Extracting the deadline keeps the meeting useful; fighting the tone or dismissing the fact both lose the data.

questions.prompt: A coach says, "You should be proud," after a child's missed kick. The line is kind, but why might it still be Parent?
choices: Because it tells the player which feeling is allowed instead of asking what happened.
Because any adult speaking to a child is automatically in Parent.
Because encouragement is less useful than criticism after failure.
questions.explanation: Nurturing Parent can sound warm while still prescribing feeling. Adult-to-child speech is not automatically Parent, and the issue is not praise versus criticism.

questions.prompt: A team lead says, "I am just stating facts: contractors from that firm are always sloppy." What concept best names the problem?
choices: Exclusion, because the lead has no access to Parent rules.
Contamination, because a Parent prejudice is presenting itself as Adult fact.
Free Child, because the lead is speaking spontaneously without a filter.
questions.explanation: The sentence claims Adult neutrality while carrying a broad judgment learned as a rule. That is contamination, not missing Parent access or playful Child spontaneity.

questions.prompt: A legal-aid coordinator feels a soft urge to say, "Do not worry, everything will be fine," even though one document is missing. Which reply fits the model best?
choices: Offer the reassurance first because warmth proves the response is not Parent.
Name the missing document and the next appointment window in plain terms.
Ask the applicant to calm down before discussing the file.
questions.explanation: Present-tense information keeps the applicant in Adult position. Warm reassurance can still manage the person's feelings, and asking for calm makes the same Parent move sharper.

questions.prompt: Two supervisors teach the model differently. One says, "Find your Adult and stay there." The other says, "Notice which state arrived before you answer." Which is the better teaching?
choices: The first, because Adult is the healthiest state and should replace the others.
The second, because state shifts are often unchosen and recognition is the first usable gain.
Both, because Parent and Child are mainly errors to remove.
questions.explanation: The model does not ask people to delete Parent or Child. It helps them notice live state shifts; Adult is useful, but healthy functioning needs range rather than one permanent setting.

reviewCards.front: A reply starts with a useful fact and ends with "you should have known." What state took over?
reviewCards.back: Parent took over the end of the sentence. The useful fact may have been Adult, but the should-and-judgment move changes the state in the room and pulls the other person toward shame or compliance.

reviewCards.front: A tense message makes you feel twelve years old for half a second. What should you label before replying?
reviewCards.back: Label the Child state that just arrived. You do not have to condemn it or obey it. Naming it gives you a chance to answer the actual present question instead of the older rank fight.

reviewCards.front: Someone speaks in a bossy tone but includes one useful deadline. What is the Adult move?
reviewCards.back: Separate the deadline from the tone. Parent delivery can carry Adult information, so extract the fact before deciding whether the tone needs a later response.

reviewCards.front: A person claims a prejudice is "just a fact." What structural problem may be happening?
reviewCards.back: That is likely contamination: one state masquerading as another. Parent judgment is wearing Adult clothing, which makes the claim sound neutral while blocking real updating.

reviewCards.front: Why is "stay in Adult all the time" a poor reading of the model?
reviewCards.back: Healthy functioning needs access to all three states. Adult checks reality, Parent holds norms and care, and Child carries feeling and play. The skill is hearing the state, not flattening yourself.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Learn to hear the state before answering the content. Parent, Adult, and Child each ask for a different kind of reply, and the conversation changes when you answer the wrong one.

ifThenPlans.plan: If feedback starts to sound like "you should have known," then point to the current data or artifact before adding any judgment.
If a practical text makes you feel small or accused, then send the concrete fact first and save the older feeling for a separate conversation.
If comfort turns into telling someone what to feel, then ask one present-tense question about what they notice or need next.
If a rule-tone enters the room, then write down the useful fact inside it before deciding whether the tone itself needs attention.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one tense sentence you heard today. Write P, A, or C beside it, then write the reply you would give if you answered from Adult.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, keep a three-column note titled Parent, Adult, Child. Add one real sentence per day under the state you heard most clearly, and review which state you answer too quickly.

memorableLines.text: Hear the voice before you answer the words.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the chapter's core skill into a short instruction the reader can use during a live exchange.

memorableLines.text: Nothing about the appointment created that sentence.
memorableLines.why: The line makes the difference between present facts and old emotional state visible without explaining it heavily.

memorableLines.text: The model does not give you a remote control.
memorableLines.why: It protects the reader from overpromising control while preserving the value of recognition.
